newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil leaves disputed Amazonian reservation as is.
newsitem.headline: Brazil leaves disputed Amazonian reservation as is.

text.p: An Amazon Indian reservation at the centre of a controversy over Brazil's Indian policy will remain the protected homeland of tribes who live there, the Brazilian government announced on Monday.

But a representative of three tribes who live on the vast Raposa/Serra do Sol reservation said the government's ruling did not lift the threat of violence and cultural obliteration faced by the Indians, principally because five towns located inside the reservation would continue to exist.

"The fact that the towns exist is a threat to us," Nelino Gale, a leader of the Makuxi tribe, told Reuters from the disputed highland region on Brazil's northern border with Venezuela and Guyana. He said 12 Indians were killed by landowners and miners between 1980 and 1995
The case of Raposa/Serra do Sol, pitting Indians against landowners and the Roraima state government, was seen as a test of Brazil's new approach to Indian reservations.

About 10 percent of Brazil's territory has been earmarked as Indian land, but many reservations have never been created because of a combination of bureaucratic hurdles and opposition from landowners and local governments.

A decree published earlier this year allowed for legal challenges to the demaraction of reservations, angering Indian groups and international organisations that support them. Most appeals have been swiftly rejected, but a handful of cases have proved difficult to decide, and Raposa/Serra do Sol was the first of those to come to judgment.

Under the ruling announced on Monday, about 50 farms located within the 5,000-square-mile (1.3 million-hectare) reservation will be returned to the local Makuxi, Apixana and Taurepang tribes, to which 12,000 people belong. An appeal by landowners and Roraima state, asking that the reservation be reduced to create mere "islands" of Indian land, was rejected.

Five small towns will be allowed to continue to exist inside Raposa/Serra do Sol, although they will be fenced off from the reservation to prevent their spread. Several farms on the edge of the reservation that the federal government gave to settlers in 1981 will also stay in private hands.
